web_evidence.title: The Confessions of Nat Turner by William Styron
web_evidence.note: The publisher explicitly states that Nat himself narrates while awaiting execution and that the story ranges across his whole life.

web_evidence.title: “It's an honorable choice:” Rebellions Against Southern Honor in William Styron's The Confessions of Nat Turner
web_evidence.note: This scholarly structural analysis describes all four novel sections as Nat's prison-frame recollections and identifies Nat as the narrator whose memories carry the reader through his past.

web_evidence.title: The Romance of Solidarity: A Long History of Sentimentalism, 1861-2009
web_evidence.note: The dissertation's Styron chapter explicitly says the novel traces Nat's life from birth to death from his first-person perspective.

web_evidence.title: Styron's Nat Turner Turns 50, Gets Religion
web_evidence.note: The University of Chicago article characterizes the novel as Nat's vivid first-person interior narrative.

web_evidence.title: Nat Turner Revisited
web_evidence.note: The full author essay contains q01488 verbatim, establishing that its white first-person voice is Styron's retrospective supplementary essay rather than a competing narrative section of the novel.

Searched “The Confessions of Nat Turner point of view first person narration structure” and “critical analysis first-person narrator Nat Turner”; opened and inspected the North Carolina State thesis and University of Washington dissertation for whole-book structural evidence.

Searched the title with “epistolary,” “frame narrative,” “multiple narrators,” and “alternating point of view”; found a prison-and-memory frame controlled by Nat, with no evidence of sustained base sections in another grammatical person.

Searched exact text from q01488 and identified it in Styron's 1992 essay “Nat Turner Revisited”; searched q01512's wording and confirmed that it belongs to the author's prefatory note rather than Nat's narration.
Checked the Penguin Random House reading guide and publisher description for coverage beyond the opening; both describe Nat's thoughts, perceptions, and life across the novel.
person_note: Nat Turner's participating 'I' controls the prison frame, remembered childhood, planning, rebellion, and approach to execution. Several event passages and dialogue-adjacent narration independently expose that voice, while two scholarly whole-book analyses and the publisher's explicit description corroborate it. Dialogue pronouns, gnomic remarks, biblical quotations, and Gray's historical document were not treated as competing narration. In particular, q01488 comes from Styron's later essay “Nat Turner Revisited,” q01512 is authorial prefatory material, and q01515 is an embedded historical source. No research indicated a sustained third- or second-person base section; the only residual uncertainty is that the Goodreads extraction mixes the novel with supplementary material from an expanded edition.
